_schema: A6 (Q5) calibration dataset for research/principle_twins.py. `positives`: 40 pairs, each two independent paraphrasings of the SAME underlying rule - a real de-identified `principle` field would clear this pair as one lesson restated. `negatives`: 40 pairs, each two DIFFERENT rules from the SAME topic - the hard case a threshold must still keep apart. Every sentence is hand-written, de-identified (no project, host, path, IP, person or version), and realistic coding-agent lesson prose - the same register the extraction prompt's FIELD principle rubric asks for.

positives.a: Don't mock the database in an integration test; run it against a real instance so a migration bug actually surfaces.
positives.b: An integration suite that mocks its own database will pass while a real migration silently breaks it - test against the genuine thing.

positives.a: Keep test fixtures independent so one test's setup can never leak into another test's assertions.
positives.b: A fixture shared across tests without isolation lets an earlier test's leftover state quietly change a later test's result.

positives.a: Retry only on transient or server errors, never on a client error that will fail identically every time.
positives.b: Retrying a 4xx response wastes calls and hides the bug - only a 5xx or a timeout is worth trying again.

positives.a: Cap retry attempts with exponential backoff so a failing dependency cannot be hammered indefinitely.
positives.b: An unbounded retry loop with no backoff turns one flaky dependency into a self-inflicted denial of service.

positives.a: Redact secrets before any text reaches persistent storage or a log line.
positives.b: A credential must be scrubbed before it is written anywhere durable, logs included, not only the primary record.

positives.a: Never commit a credential to version control, even in a throwaway branch that will be deleted.
positives.b: A secret checked into any branch, however temporary, is effectively public - history does not forget.

positives.a: Invalidate a cache entry the moment its source of truth changes, rather than relying on a time-based expiry alone.
positives.b: A cache that only expires on a timer will keep serving a stale answer long after the underlying data moved.

positives.a: Key a cache by every input that affects the result, or two different queries will silently share one answer.
positives.b: Leaving one relevant parameter out of the cache key makes the cache return the wrong answer for a query it never actually saw.

positives.a: Hold a lock for the shortest possible critical section to avoid starving other writers.
positives.b: A critical section that does more work than it needs to starves every other writer waiting on the same lock.

positives.a: Re-read shared state after acquiring a lock; a value read before the lock can be stale by the time you actually have it.
positives.b: A value fetched before taking the lock may already be wrong once the lock is held - read again inside the critical section.

positives.a: Give every config value read from the environment a safe fallback instead of raising at import time.
positives.b: A misconfigured environment variable should degrade to a sane default, not crash the whole process on startup.

positives.a: Validate a config value's type at the boundary, not deep inside the code that eventually uses it.
positives.b: Checking a setting's type where it enters the system, rather than wherever it happens to be used, catches a bad value before it can do damage.

positives.a: Catch the narrowest exception type you can actually recover from; a bare except hides real bugs.
positives.b: A blanket except clause swallows genuine failures along with the one you meant to handle - catch only what you can actually fix.

positives.a: Log an error with enough context to reproduce it, not just the exception's bare message.
positives.b: An error log with no surrounding context is nearly useless for reproducing the failure later - capture the state around it too.

positives.a: Make a migration backward compatible so the old code can still run during a rolling deploy.
positives.b: A schema change must keep working with the previous version of the code, or a rolling deploy breaks mid-rollout.

positives.a: Never run a schema migration and a large data backfill in the same transaction.
positives.b: Bundling a structural change with a big backfill in one transaction risks locking the table for the whole operation - split them.

positives.a: Never log a raw request body that might contain personal data.
positives.b: A request body can carry personal information, so it must never be written into a log verbatim.

positives.a: Use structured logging so a field can be queried later instead of grepped out of free text.
positives.b: A log line as a structured record, not free-form text, is what makes a later query for one field actually possible.

positives.a: Rate limit by the caller's identity, not by IP address, or one user behind a shared proxy blocks everyone else.
positives.b: Limiting by IP rather than by account punishes every user sharing that address once one of them is throttled.

positives.a: Return a clear retry-after signal when throttling a client, rather than a bare rejection.
positives.b: A throttled response should tell the caller when to try again, not just refuse the request with no guidance.

positives.a: Free a large buffer as soon as its last use is done, not at the end of the function.
positives.b: Holding onto a big allocation past its last real use wastes memory for the rest of the function's lifetime - release it early.

positives.a: Profile before optimizing memory use; a guess about what is expensive is usually wrong.
positives.b: Optimizing memory from a guess instead of a profile usually targets the wrong allocation entirely - measure first.

positives.a: Pin a dependency's exact version in a lockfile so a build is reproducible months later.
positives.b: Without an exact pinned version in a lockfile, the same build command can silently resolve a different dependency tree later.

positives.a: Review what a new dependency actually does before adding it, not just its popularity.
positives.b: A dependency's star count says nothing about what its code actually does - read it before you add it.

positives.a: Make an API idempotent so a client's retry after a timeout cannot double the effect.
positives.b: If a call is not idempotent, a client retrying after a timeout can apply the same effect twice without either side knowing.

positives.a: Version a public API explicitly rather than silently changing behavior under the same endpoint.
positives.b: Changing a public endpoint's behavior without a new version number breaks every client that trusted the old contract.

positives.a: Review a diff for what it removes, not only what it adds; a deletion can silently drop a guard.
positives.b: A reviewer who only reads the added lines can miss a deleted safety check that the diff quietly removed.

positives.a: A review comment should say why a change is wrong, not just that it is wrong.
positives.b: Flagging a line without explaining the reason leaves the author unable to actually fix the underlying problem.

positives.a: Roll a deploy out to a small percentage of traffic before shipping it everywhere.
positives.b: Shipping a change to all traffic at once skips the chance to catch a regression on a small slice first.

positives.a: Keep a fast, tested rollback path for every deploy, not just a forward migration plan.
positives.b: A deploy plan that only goes forward leaves no fast way out when the new version turns out to be broken.

positives.a: Alert on a symptom the user would notice, not on every internal metric that happens to move.
positives.b: Paging on every internal metric that moves buries the alert that actually matters under noise nobody reads.

positives.a: A dashboard should show the trend over time, not just the current value, or a slow regression goes unnoticed.
positives.b: Showing only the current value on a dashboard hides a slow, steady regression that a trend line would have caught.

positives.a: Validate input at the boundary where it enters the system, not deep inside a function that assumes it is already safe.
positives.b: A function deep in the call stack that trusts its input unchecked is only as safe as the boundary that let the input in.

positives.a: Default to the most restrictive permission and widen it deliberately, not the other way around.
positives.b: Starting with a permissive default and narrowing it later leaves a window where too much access is granted by accident.

positives.a: Keep a commit to one logical change so a later revert does not also undo something unrelated.
positives.b: A commit that bundles two unrelated changes forces a future revert to either undo both or hand-untangle them.

positives.a: Write a commit message that explains why a change was made, not just what changed.
positives.b: The diff already shows what changed - a commit message earns its place by saying why the change was necessary.

positives.a: Measure the ratio of costs on a hostile input, not the absolute time, to tell linear from quadratic.
positives.b: A raw timing number cannot separate linear from quadratic - compare how the cost SCALES as the input grows instead.

positives.a: Batch many small operations into one call when the fixed cost per call dominates the work itself.
positives.b: When each call's overhead outweighs the actual work, combining many small calls into one batch removes that repeated cost.

positives.a: Document the reasoning behind a non-obvious decision, not just the decision itself.
positives.b: Recording only the decision and not the reasoning behind it leaves a future reader unable to tell if the situation has changed enough to revisit it.

positives.a: Keep an example in the documentation runnable, or it silently rots the first time the API changes.
positives.b: A documentation example that is never actually executed drifts out of date the moment the underlying API changes.
